name: Whiplash-Associated Disorder (WAD)
summary: Neck symptoms following acceleration–deceleration trauma, commonly a road traffic collision; classify severity and screen carefully for associated injury.

looksLike: Dizziness or concentration difficulty may coexist
redFlags: Midline tenderness or high-risk trauma requiring Canadian C-Spine Rule assessment
Loss of consciousness, severe headache or repeated vomiting
Progressive weakness, sensory loss, gait change
Airway, swallowing, vascular or spinal cord symptoms
firstSteps: Exclude serious injury and classify WAD grade
Provide reassurance, clear information and encouragement to resume ordinary activity as tolerated
Use gentle active movement and avoid unnecessary immobilisation

assess: Possible neurological findings in WAD III

tests.name: Canadian C-Spine Rule (clinician decision aid)
tests.purpose: Determine need for cervical spine imaging in alert, stable adults after blunt trauma; apply the complete validated rule.
tests.positive: Any high-risk criterion, or inability to rotate 45° when the rule indicates rotation testing.

stages.label: Protection, Education & Symptom-Guided Loading
stages.goal: Address safety, settle excessive irritability and maintain useful movement.
do: Exclude serious injury and classify WAD grade
Provide reassurance, clear information and encouragement to resume ordinary activity as tolerated
Use gentle active movement and avoid unnecessary immobilisation
Address sleep, headache, dizziness or concussion symptoms through appropriate referral pathways
dose: Comfortable cervical ROM: 5–10 reps several times/day
Walking: begin with tolerable short bouts, build gradually
moveOn: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.

stages.label: Mobility, Strength & Capacity
stages.goal: Restore the specific strength, mobility and control required by the condition.
when: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.
do: Progress cervical and scapular endurance and strength
Graded aerobic activity and functional exposure
Treat associated vestibular or sensorimotor impairments when identified
dose: Deep neck flexor endurance and scapular strengthening: 2–3 sets, 3 days/week
Aerobic activity: frequent low-to-moderate intensity bouts as tolerated
moveOn: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.

stages.label: Functional Restoration & Return to Activity
stages.goal: Rebuild real-world, occupational or sporting capacity.
when: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.
do: Progress driving, work and sport-specific demands
Increase lifting, rotation and sustained activity gradually
Coordinate multidisciplinary care for persistent disability or high distress
dose: Progress activity volume in small steps, avoiding repeated symptom exacerbation
moveOn: Full task exposure is completed progressively.
No clinically meaningful deterioration during the following 24 hours.

returnCriteria: Functional neck movement and neurological status stable

structures: Cervical muscles, joints and other soft tissues; neurological structures may be involved in higher-grade presentations.
mechanism: Symptoms may emerge or evolve over hours after collision
classification: WAD 0: no neck complaint or signs
WAD I: pain/stiffness without physical signs
investigations: Use validated trauma decision rules and urgent medical referral when indicated.
Imaging is determined by trauma risk and clinical findings, not pain intensity alone.
manual: Gentle mobilization may be considered after serious injury is excluded and when it supports active recovery.
Avoid forceful cervical techniques in acute trauma or when vascular/neurological concerns exist.
modalities: Analgesia decisions belong with the prescribing clinician.
Passive treatment should not replace advice, activity and graded exercise.
mistakes: Applying routine neck treatment before trauma screening
Ignoring concussion, dizziness or psychological distress
pearls: Use the Canadian C-Spine Rule only in its intended population and setting.
Recovery is influenced by physical, cognitive and psychosocial factors; avoid deterministic predictions.

tests.name: Canadian C-Spine Rule (clinician decision aid)
tests.purpose: Determine need for cervical spine imaging in alert, stable adults after blunt trauma; apply the complete validated rule.
tests.positive: Any high-risk criterion, or inability to rotate 45° when the rule indicates rotation testing.
tests.patientPosition: Assess alert, stable adult trauma patient; document high-risk factors, low-risk factors and ability to rotate 45° each way.
tests.therapistPosition: Position yourself to observe and stabilise the relevant segment without forcing the movement.
tests.handPlacement: Use comfortable, controlled contact appropriate to the test; avoid painful compression or excessive force.
procedure: Explain the test and obtain consent.
Screen contraindications and compare sides when appropriate.
Perform the movement slowly and apply only the required resistance or stress.
Record familiar symptom reproduction, range, strength and side-to-side difference.
tests.interpretation: Follow the rule and local trauma pathway; do not use in populations outside its validated scope.
tests.clinicalNote: A special test modifies clinical probability; it does not confirm a diagnosis in isolation.
